newsitem.title: UK: World refining overcapacity seen ending.
newsitem.headline: World refining overcapacity seen ending.

text.p: The world's oil refining industry is beginning to emerge from nearly two decades of poor returns and overcapacity but Europe will continue to experience a surplus of gasoline for some years to come, a leading industry analyst said on Tuesday.

"In our view that structural surplus, that huge overcapacity, which lasted for 15 to 20 years, has come to an end," Steve Terry, managing director of London-based Petroleum Economics Ltd, told the Oil and Money conference.
From running at 60 percent of capacity in the early 1980s, every refinery would have to produce at about 87 percent of capacity every day of this year to keep pace with growing demand, he said.
Capacity utilisation would have to rise to nearly 94 percent by the end of the decade and five years later there could be a shortage of refining capacity, Terry added.
"It's a much better business than it has been in the past," he said.
But recent heavy investment in cracking capacity, unexpected increases in light sweet crude supply and rising diesel sales were continuing to create a surplus of gasoline in Europe.
"The surplus of gasoline is likely to continue for some time," Terry said.
But exports to the U.S. where gasoline demand growth was more robust provided an outlet for European refineries despite tough new environmental laws due by the year 2000.
